events.text: Your usual seat at the Moon Pavilion has been given to a minor scribe, and nobody apologises. The wind-chimes along the White Stairs, which have rung for you at every dawn since your elevation, hang silent today, as if listening for someone else. {hn4_n} Houses would be glad to see you fall, you realise, and {npc} has not looked at you once all week.

choices.text: Count which Houses sent no midsummer gifts

effects.log: It takes an afternoon and a very patient steward. Seven Houses sent nothing. All seven share a cousin, a creditor, or a grudge. You draw lines between them, and the drawing begins to look like a net.

choices.text: Blame the weather, and take your tea

effects.log: The tea is good. The chimes stay quiet till the evening, when a runner hurries along the stairs and sets them swinging, and you decide it was only practice.

events.text: A petition is entered at the Jade Court: {hn4_charge}, in a clerk's perfect hand, backed by two seals that are real and one that is a lovely imitation. {hn4_court} will hear it when the plum trees bloom. It would be funny if it were not so well timed. {npc} was the last to leave the Lotus Ledger room on the night the seals were stamped.

choices.text: Lay the three seals side by side beneath a lamp

effects.log: The false one is almost perfect. Almost. A single petal of the lotus is drawn from memory by someone who has only ever seen the real one at a distance. You wrap the proof in silk.

choices.text: Send a courteous reply, and go on with the season

effects.log: The reply is courteous. The season goes on. The plum trees bud early that year, as if impatient, and you walk beneath them with a lighter step than you should have.

events.text: A ledger-clerk, paid in plum wine, copied the minutes. A boatman remembered the night barges. Between them you have everything: {npc} stands behind {hn4_n} others, and the thread runs through the Jade Court's Rolls, a Ministry stamp, and a loan from a faction that swore it was neutral. Spread across your floor in the lamplight it looks like the map of a city you used to love.

choices.text: Strike first, while they are still arguing over dinner

effects.log: You move on the night of the Harvest Dinner, when every plotter is at a different table. It is swift, and loud, and ugly, and you wake the next morning to find that it is also over.

choices.text: Send gifts and a polite summons, and make a quiet peace

effects.log: The gifts are tasteful. The summons is warm. By the third cup of tea the plot has come apart like wet paper, and no one at the table will admit it ever had a shape.

choices.text: Accept the next invitation to the Lotus Pavilion, and bring your own tea

effects.log: You go in white, with a flask under your arm. If they mean to close the lid, you would like to see their faces while they do.

events.text: The invitation reads like any other: a banquet at the Lotus Pavilion, a table for twelve, your seat by the lake. The lake is the wrong colour. The doors close behind you, and the cranes on the roof go quiet. {npc} lifts a cup at the far end of the table, among {hn4_n} others, none of them smiling. The dishes are placed so that no one sits with their back to a wall but you.

choices.text: Overturn the table, and go straight for {npc}

ok.log: The table goes over with a crash of porcelain. The lake ripples. When the dust settles, the doors are open, the guests are scattered, and {npc} is sitting on the floor, smiling at nothing.

fail.log: The table goes over, and so do you. The guests are quicker than their robes suggest. You are pinned against a pillar with a bruised rib and a very polite verdict being read.

choices.text: Bow to the table, and leave by the water-stair

effects.log: The water-stair is long and green and slippery. Nobody follows. At the bottom a boat is waiting, which you did not order, and you are too tired to wonder who did.

events.text: It is over by the time the lake settles. The Lotus Pavilion is silent but for the drip of a cracked lantern, and {npc} kneels on the wet stone among {hn4_n} others in a long, bowed row. Nobody speaks. A pavilion cat comes out to sniff the hem of your robe and sits against your ankle. You had thought you would feel more.

choices.text: Spare them, and send them home with only their seals taken

effects.log: They go. Some of them weep. One of them, at the gate, stops and looks back, and you think they will say something. They do not. The cat follows you in.

choices.text: Have their names struck from every House ledger

effects.log: The clerks are very quick. By the next moon the names are blank in forty books, and no one on the Isles recalls what they were. It is done, and it is cold.

events.text: They are kind about it, in the way of people who have already spent the money. The Court reads the charges, the clerks stamp three copies, and a young Ministry runner is sent to take your seat-token, and cannot make themself look at you. {npc} stays in the gallery to the end, a fold of silk in both hands, and leaves before the last stamp.

choices.text: Hand over the seat-token yourself, before it is asked

effects.log: The runner takes it in both hands, as if it were hot. The clerks look relieved. You walk down the White Stairs on your own feet, and the chimes, as you pass, ring once.

choices.text: Ask for a copy of every stamped page

effects.log: They give them. Forty pages, each in a perfect hand. You read all forty on the lower stair, and find one small crack in the whole: a date that cannot be right. You keep it.

events.text: The lower dock at midnight smells of wet rope and lamp-oil. A ferry-keeper with a lantern on their hat asks where you are bound, and you cannot say. They take you anyway, for the price of a story, and you give them the one about the chimes. The ferry pulls out into the dark, and above you the lights of the Isles go on being beautiful. {npc} took your seat before the ferry cast off.

choices.text: Tell the ferry-keeper about the chimes, and keep nothing back

effects.log: The ferry-keeper listens as one listens to the weather. At the far landing they say only: "That is a good story for a bad year." You carry the sentence like a coin.

choices.text: Watch the Isles shrink until the cloud closes over them

effects.log: They shrink. They are, for a moment, a handful of bright coins on a dark cloth. Then the cloud closes. You sit with your hands open on your knees and breathe.

events.text: The peace is signed on a pale blue scroll with a pressed lotus in the fold. {npc} and {hn4_n} others bow in a line on the terrace, and you bow back, exactly as deep. A cake is passed round. Everyone eats a little, as people eat at the funeral of a thing nobody quite liked. Afterward you find a card under your cup. It says only: "Until the next harvest."

choices.text: Keep the card in your sleeve and read it every moon

effects.log: You read it every moon. It does not change. You do, a little, each time, and by the harvest you could recite it in your sleep.

choices.text: Pay the next harvest's courtesy early, and in full

effects.log: The courtesy is paid. The card is returned, torn neatly in half. Whether this is thanks or insult, you will not know till spring.

events.text: Ten years later the lower ferry sets you down at your own landing. The tea-seller's stall is gone, and a small shrine to nobody stands in its place. Your House gates are open and the courtyard has been swept. The chimes along the White Stairs, silent when you left, are ringing again, thinly, in the wind. An old cook has been waiting longer than anyone should, and hands you a bowl without a word.

choices.text: Eat, and ask nothing about the years

effects.log: You eat. The cook says nothing about the years, and neither do you. The chimes go on. By the second bowl you realise you are home.

choices.text: Climb the White Stairs first, and ring every chime

effects.log: They ring. Forty of them, each one a little sharp. By the top you are laughing and out of breath, and a clerk at the gate pretends not to see.

events.text: You come back in winter, on a borrowed barge, with the same sword. The Rolls have your name again, in smaller ink, and your seat is under snow. Runners bow to you on the stairs, carefully. Nobody mentions the ten years. The House has learned a new way to be polite, and you take a long time to learn it back.

choices.text: Greet every servant by name, one at a time

effects.log: It takes an hour. At the end of it the snow has stopped, and half the household has remembered how to laugh.

choices.text: Clear your own seat of snow, and sit in it first

effects.log: The snow is cold and the seat is colder. You sit. Someone, wordlessly, brings a quilt. You decide that is as good a welcome as any.

events.text: The sacred lamps on the high altar have burned a hair lower every dusk for a month, and nobody can find the leak. A god of the next shrine, who sends figs at every turning of the year, has sent nothing. The oldest priest turns away at the offering. {hn4_n} gods would see you fall, you realise, and {npc} has not come to the evening rite once.

choices.text: Ask the temple clerks which shrines have been quietly visited

effects.log: The clerks are shy and exact. Seven shrines have had unexpected callers, always at dusk, always with a gift of rice. You write the list in the margin of your prayers, and begin to draw lines.

choices.text: Refill the lamps, and call it a thin season

effects.log: The lamps are refilled. They burn level for a week. Then one gutters again, in the middle of the night, and the temple cat regards you from the altar-step with open pity.

events.text: A Transgression is entered in the Book of Fates: {hn4_charge}, in the Keeper's own hand, witnessed by two real gods and one false. {hn4_court} will hear it when the cranes fly north. It is nonsense, and costly nonsense. {npc} was seen leaving the Hall of Names at dusk, with ink on a sleeve and a face as smooth as river stone.

choices.text: Trace the ink on the false witness's seal

effects.log: The ink is the ordinary black of the Hall of Names, but it has been thinned with something floral. You smell it in the temple stores, in a cask of incense-oil that is not yours. It narrows the list.

choices.text: Trust the Book to see through it

effects.log: You trust it. The Book is old and busy, and has seen through very little in its time. The cranes fly north earlier than expected, and the hearing is on you before you have finished your tea.

events.text: A river-sprite who owes you a favour, a clerk of the Book who loves figs, and a priest who cannot keep a secret have between them given you everything: names, dates, debts of faith. {npc} stands behind {hn4_n} others, and the thread passes through a rival pantheon's seal to an Elder Lineage you thought neutral. In the lamplight the list looks like the roots of a banyan, and a decision waits at the end of every root.

choices.text: Strike first, before the next new moon

effects.log: You act on the eve of the new moon, when every plotter is kneeling at a different altar. It is quick, and loud, and unlovely, and by dawn the roots are dug up and lying in the sun.

choices.text: Offer their shrines a generous covenant of offerings

effects.log: The covenant is generous. By the third bowl of rice-wine the plot has come apart, and no god at the table will admit it ever had a shape. It is, in its way, the finest piece of work you have done.

choices.text: Go to the next feast they hold, wearing white

effects.log: You go in white, with a flask of your own wine. If they mean to close the lid, you would like to see their faces while they do it.

events.text: The feast is laid beneath the great ginkgo: forty cushions, no guards. The pavilion doors close with a sound like a held breath, and the lanterns do not sway. {npc} raises a bowl of rice-wine from the far side, among {hn4_n} others, all of them smiling in the way of gods who have already agreed. The ginkgo drops one leaf, very slowly.

choices.text: Throw down the cushions, and go straight for {npc}

ok.log: The cushions fly. The lanterns swing. When the ginkgo has shed its second leaf, the doors are open, the feast is scattered, and {npc} sits on the floor, bowl in hand, no longer smiling.

fail.log: The cushions fly, and so do you. The gods are quicker than their mantles suggest. You are pinned against the ginkgo's trunk, bruised at the ribs, while a Transgression is read in a soft voice.

choices.text: Bow, take your cup, and leave by the garden gate

effects.log: The garden gate is low and overgrown. Nobody follows. Outside, the lane is empty and smells of rain, and you walk it for a long time with a cup still in your hand.

events.text: The ginkgo is bare by the time it is over. {npc} and {hn4_n} others sit on the cold flagstones in a row, and the rice-wine has spilled and dried. Nobody speaks. A temple dog comes out to sniff the hem of your mantle and sits, politely, against your leg. You had thought you would feel more.

choices.text: Spare them, and send them home with their offering-bowls

effects.log: They go. Some of them weep. One of them, at the gate, stops and looks back, and you think they will say something. They do not. The dog follows you in.

choices.text: Strike their names from every shrine register

effects.log: The scribes are very quick. By the next moon the names are blank in forty books, and no god recalls what they were. It is done, and it is cold.

events.text: The Court is courteous in its efficiency. The Transgression is read, three witnesses nod, and the Keeper of Names draws a line through you with a brush barely wet. A young attendant carries your lamp away. {npc} bows to the dais with the others, and then, alone in the whole gallery, stays bowed a breath too long.

choices.text: Take your own lamp from the attendant, and carry it out

effects.log: The attendant gives it up, startled. You carry it down the long hall, and it burns steady the whole way, which no one in the gallery quite forgives.

choices.text: Ask for a copy of the Transgression, with the witnesses named

effects.log: They give it. Forty pages, each in a perfect hand. You read them on the lower road, and find one small crack: a date that cannot be right. You keep it.

events.text: At the lowest ferry the lamps are already lit. The ferry-keeper asks nothing, and a pilgrim waiting on the bench shares a bowl of cold barley without a word. The boat pulls out into the dark. Behind you the temple lights go on being beautiful, and one by one the faithful on the shore turn away. {npc} sits in your place at the altar.

choices.text: Share the barley with the pilgrim, and ask nothing

effects.log: The barley is cold and wholesome. At the far landing the pilgrim gives a small bow and says: "A good year to be lost." You carry that sentence like a coin.

choices.text: Look at the temple's lamps one last time, and name each one

effects.log: There are forty. You name them, in order, under your breath, and by the thirtieth you have stopped feeling cheated. The cloud closes over the last.

events.text: The covenant is sealed with a plum branch and a bowl of salt. {npc} and {hn4_n} others take it kneeling and rise smiling. The eastern shrines will send you figs again at the new year. A priest asks at the door whether peace tastes as you expected. It tastes like a very good soup that has been left to cool.

choices.text: Keep the plum branch on the altar, and watch it every moon

effects.log: The branch does not blossom. It does not wither. By the harvest you know its every knot, and you are, you suspect, a little wiser for it.

choices.text: Send a small gift each season, and say nothing about the soup

effects.log: The gifts are accepted. The soup goes on cooling in the corner of your mind, but the temple is quiet, and the figs arrive on time.

events.text: Ten years later the lower ferry sets you down at your own landing. The lamp-seller's stall is gone, and a small shrine to no one stands in its place. Your temple's doors are open, the high altar is swept, and the sacred lamps burn at the right height again. An old cook, who has been waiting longer than anyone should, hands you a bowl without a word.

choices.text: Eat, and ask nothing about the years

effects.log: You eat. The cook says nothing about the years, and neither do you. The lamps burn level. By the second bowl you realise you are home.

choices.text: Walk the cloister first, and touch every pillar

effects.log: The pillars are warm. At the fortieth there is a new chip in the stone, and you put your thumb in it, and a lamp you cannot see flares in welcome.

events.text: You come home on a wet evening with a pilgrim's staff and no escort. The Book of Fates has your name again, in smaller ink. At the gate the oldest priest looks up, blinks, and quietly lights every lamp in the cloister, one by one, until the whole temple is gold. Nobody mentions the ten years. The faithful have learned a new way to be polite.

choices.text: Thank each priest by name, one at a time

effects.log: It takes an hour. At the end of it the rain has stopped, and half the temple has remembered how to laugh.

choices.text: Stand in the rain before the high altar until the lamps dry your mantle

effects.log: You stand. The lamps warm the air. Someone, wordlessly, brings a dry shawl. You decide that is as good a welcome as any.
